answer: Time is unique and always moves forward, so return the current epoch ms. Works on exactly one machine, as long as the function is never called twice in the same millisecond (else go to micro/nanoseconds).
Both return 1729: collision, not globally unique. Fix: concatenate machine ID and epoch ms: m1-1729, m2-1729.
Whenever two IDs collide, add to the ID the thing that caused the collision.
evidence: §1.4 "That is the standard way to resolve a collision"

answer: Multiple threads on several cores can call the function in the same millisecond and both get m1-1729.
First add the thread ID (m1-t1-1729); then replace it with a static (shared, atomic) counter.
concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()) -> m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729 (m2-t1-1729, m2-t3-1729).
Appending every cause of a collision makes IDs gigantic (a part per cause); one counter beats any number of threads.
A single variable per process, shared by every thread; it must be incremented atomically (counter++ is read-add-write; use a lock or atomic integer).
The counter already grows on every call, so the time part adds nothing; strike it out. ID = concat(machine_id, counter++): m1-01, m1-02, m2-01...
The counter's size: unsigned 32-bit stops ~4.29 billion, signed ~2.1 billion; 64-bit (~1.8e19) effectively endless.
It comes back as 0 and reissues m1-01, m1-02 (duplicates). Root cause: the counter lives in volatile memory with no copy.
Back the counter up to a file: counter = load() once at start; in get_id, counter++, save_counter(counter) on every call, return concat(machine_id, counter).
Thousands of tiny disk writes a second (disk IO overload), and every ID waits on a disk write instead of coming from memory (latency). (Plus fsync needed to be durable makes each save expensive.)

Presented as one of "two good ways": one disk write per boot, counter in memory never saved. Downsides: startup increment must be atomic and every ID carries one more part (longer ID, index cost per ch 5).

Read the counter (say 1), add 1,000, store that, hand out the next thousand from memory; when you reach the stored value add another 1,000 and store again. Writes ahead, so after a crash start from the stored value.
const N = 1000; int counter = load() + N; save_counter(counter); func get_id() { counter++; if (counter % N == 0) save_counter(counter); return concat(machine_id, counter); }
Disk writes behind: what is on disk was already handed out and up to N more may have gone out since the last flush, so start past the whole window.
Cuts disk IO a thousandfold; implement as a mod check (counter % N == 0) on each call, not a timer thread.
Disk holds 3 then 6 (6 at crash, 8 handed out). Safe restart value 10 = 6 + 3 + 1 (load()+N = 9, first ++ gives 10); save new start before handing out.
9 is never used (some numbers skipped). Acceptable: skipped integers cost nothing, a duplicate ID can cost an order; correctness matters more than using every integer.
(1) Correctness of the system matters more than using every integer (unused numbers fine, duplicate not). (2) Whenever a machine recovers, start from the safest value (last saved + N + 1).
Conflict resolution in multi-master: T1 sets a=20, T2 sets a=30 on a=10; with newer-write-wins, the larger ID marks the newer write, keep a=30.
No. Larger, not next: 1,2,5,7,8,9,32 qualifies; gaps allowed. Gap-free is "sequential".

Time in the most significant (left) digits means IDs come out in time order; machine and counter only break ties within a ms. Board/figure: time on the left "decides the order: most significant part, makes sorting simple".
Inside one millisecond order can flip: request to machine 2 then machine 1 gives 17290002 then 17290001.
Nearly free: nothing shared, any machine can serve a request, no central state, excellent throughput; IDs sort roughly by creation time.
Clock synchronization against NTP servers via a daemon (chronyd/ntpd) that runs all the time, slewing the clock toward true time.
Hardware quartz crystal whose vibration frequency shifts with temperature (~±20 ppm, ~2 s/day), so each clock drifts at its own rate.
232, 244, 237, 239; the third (237) is smaller than the second (244): not monotonically increasing because m4's clock is 1 ms ahead.

Strict order when ID logic runs on many machines is almost impossible (not a theorem, but too many things break it).
One machine runs get_id() (time-first, one clock); clients make a network call to it and get an ID back; it never issues below its last ID.

One generator means no skew between generators. When sync finds the clock ahead it doesn't jump back; it slows the clock until real time catches up (large errors, >128 ms in ntpd, are stepped; so generator never goes below last value, waits or refuses).
Single point of failure: if it or its disk fails, no order can be created. Fix: add a second server behind a load balancer.

Let MySQL's auto-increment be the ID service (ticket server): keep one row, replace it per request so auto-increment gives the next value. Delete+insert in one transaction is costly; use an upsert (REPLACE) instead.
INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE updates the existing row in place; REPLACE INTO deletes the old row and inserts a new one (usually slower, ~32x in one benchmark).

Dummy column with a constant: you can't insert a row with no values, so stub gives the insert something to write and hits the unique key.
